think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 35-year-old man presents with progressive mononeuropathy multiplex features—specifically severe ulnar and medial cutaneous nerve dysfunction, palpable nerve thickening, and marked intrinsic hand weakness—without any cutaneous hypopigmented or erythematous lesions. Surprisingly, he exhibits brisk generalized hyperreflexia (3+) and extensive neurography findings of cervical myelitis, ganglionitis, and radiculitis, mimicking a primary central demyelinating disease, neurosarcoidosis, or compressive brachial plexopathy, obscuring an atypical pure neural infectious neuropathy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs after physical and neurological examination and initial bedside nerve ultrasonography revealing marked fascicular enlargement of the right ulnar and medial cutaneous nerves, but prior to spinal MRI neurography, lumbar puncture CSF studies, PET scanning, and nerve biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Isolated compressive ulnar neuropathy (cubital tunnel syndrome) is ruled out by proximal nerve enlargement extending into the axilla, medial cutaneous nerve involvement, and brisk global reflexes (3+). Demyelinating CNS disorders (multiple sclerosis, NMOSD) and autoimmune neuropathies are excluded by negative aquaporin-4, MOG, and antiganglioside antibodies, along with normal CSF IgG index and absent oligoclonal bands. Neurosarcoidosis is excluded by negative serum ACE and absence of mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy on chest CT. The diagnosis of pure neural Hansen's disease (leprosy) is confirmed by nerve biopsy demonstrating acid-fast bacilli on Wade-Fite staining within foamy histiocytes.
case_prompt:
A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 5-month history of progressive paresthesia along the medial aspect of the right forearm and hand. One month after symptom onset, he developed hypoesthesia in the same anatomical distribution, accompanied by weakness and abduction of the fourth and fifth digits of his right hand. Around the same time, he noted a nodular swelling proximal to the medial epicondyle of the right upper extremity that was painless at rest but tender upon palpation. His past medical history was notable only for surgical resection of a benign oncocytoma in the right parotid gland 1.5 years earlier; he took no regular medications and had no known drug allergies.

On physical examination, complete dermatological inspection revealed no skin lesions or hypopigmented macules. Neurological examination revealed palpable thickening of the right ulnar nerve superior to the elbow. Palpation of the ulnar nerve elicited severe shock-like paresthesias and pain with prominent allodynia. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk globally (3+). Sensory testing demonstrated intact proprioception, vibration, and discriminative sensation; however, light touch was diminished, and pinprick and temperature sensations were completely abolished in the right ulnar nerve distribution. Hypoesthesia was also identified over the sensory territory of the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm. Motor examination revealed Medical Research Council (MRC) grade 3/5 strength in the right first dorsal interosseous and abductor digiti minimi muscles. Cranial nerves were intact, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory evaluation revealed normal complete blood count, normal serum biochemistry, and normal inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. High-resolution ultrasonography of the upper extremity demonstrated marked enlargement of the cross-sectional area of both the right ulnar nerve (1.12 cm³) and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (45 mm³) extending continuously from the proximal forearm to the axilla, with homogeneous fascicular dilatation, hypoechogenicity, loss of intraneural architecture, and positive flow on Power Doppler, while contralateral nerve measurements and the brachial plexus appeared normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome / Compressive Ulnar Neuropathy
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Although the patient presented with ulnar clawing and tenderness at the medial epicondyle, isolated compressive entrapment cannot explain the proximal extension of nerve thickening to the axilla, concomitant medial cutaneous antebrachial neuropathy, generalized hyperreflexia, or subsequent imaging evidence of myelitis and radiculitis.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Central Demyelinating Disease (Multiple Sclerosis / Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Extensive cervical myelitis extending from C2 to D3 with ganglionitis raised suspicion for primary neuroinflammatory demyelinating disease, but specific autoantibodies were negative and CSF showed no oligoclonal bands with normal IgG index.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: No neoplastic cells or IgG oligoclonal bands were detected, and the IgG index was normal... Anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and anti-aquaporin-4 antibody tests were also negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Sarcoidosis can cause cranial and peripheral neuropathy, radiculitis, and myelitis; however, serum ACE was negative and chest imaging showed no hilar lymphadenopathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Computed tomography of the chest showed small streaks of fibrosis in the upper lobes, while the remaining lung parenchyma showed no significant changes. No evidence of lymph node enlargement or pleural effusion was observed... angiotensin-I-converting enzyme (ACE) tests were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Pure Neural Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive diagnosis was confirmed histopathologically on ultrasound-guided biopsy of the right medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which showed endoneurial and epineurial mononuclear infiltrates with foamy macrophages containing acid-fast bacilli on Wade-Fite staining, satisfying criteria for confirmed pure neural leprosy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: These changes included the presence of a mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate (with foamy macrophages) in the epineurium, perineurium, and endoneurium; fibrosis in the epineurium and endoneurium; the absence of myelin fibers (observed in semithin sections); and the presence of acid-fast bacilli in foamy macrophages (Wade-Fite stain, 1+/4+)... classified as 'category 1: confirmed diagnosis.'

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic teaching case formulated following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt stops prior to spinal neurography and biopsy.
